nodes.text: Judgement Day — The River
The street outside the windshield goes soft and wet. Streetlights stretch into long reflections and the reflections turn into water. Judgement Day isn't on a road anymore.
The tires make the noise of oars.
Faust has both hands on the wheel, which is now a tiller, which is now a wheel again.
(watching the water out the window) So we're a boat.
Longboat. You said it the other day. Take the longboat out, prowl uncertain waters.
I was being colorful.
You're always being colorful. It keeps happening.
On the shore, things go by. A strip mall. A Little League diamond with the lights still on. A tanooki leaf drifting down onto the water and floating there.
I know that ball field.
Grand slam. I was nine. That's not your ball field that's my ball field.
It's everybody's ball field. Every ball field looks like that.
Then it's everybody's grand slam. I'll allow it.
A figure on the bank raises a hand like he's hailing a cab. Faust slows the boat without meaning to.
Don't stop for every hitchhiker. They aren't yours.
How do I know which ones are mine.
They'll have exact change.
Faust lets the figure slide by. It waves again, patient, unbothered, used to it.
Okay hold up. Faust. I'm going to say a thing. You're driving the boat on the river with dead dudes waving at you.
I noticed.
You told Deborah, I feel like Charon ferrying and she said aptly put and now look.
That was a joke about pills.
Funny how jokes keep coming home to roost.
So who's paying the fare. Charon gets a coin. Coin on the eyes, coin under the tongue. History major. I know these things.
Faust pats his pockets. Receipts. A pen from work. A single blister-pack pill he doesn't remember pocketing.
I've got one Advil.
Ferryman's got to eat.
The water ahead is darker. A toll gate rises out of it, an old wooden arm painted red and white, a booth with nobody in it. The radio in the dash turns on by itself.
(over the radio, bored, kind) toll is something personal. can't sell what isn't personal. you said that. I heard you say that to the mirror.
You were in the back.
walls are thin at a drugstore.
What counts as personal.
you know already. you're stalling.
Faust thinks about it. He pulls Judgement Day up to the booth.

(to the empty booth) Here's one. I've been telling people my grand-dad was either Jack Parsons or L. Ron Hubbard. Rocket fuel on one side, sailor boy on the other. And I tell it like a party trick, because it's a great story. But the personal part is I don't know. I really don't know whose I am.
I tell the story so nobody sees me not knowing.
Silence. Then the gate arm lifts.
that'll do.
(quietly) Damn, man.
Sailor boy it is. Look at you. You're steering.
I'm steering.
They go under the arm. Behind them it drops back down. The water goes still and very flat and very bright, a fluorescent kind of bright, and up ahead a building sits on the water with every light on.
